STEP 0 — DEEP RESEARCH FIRST (DO THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — MANDATORY)
Before writing a single word of narration or any image prompt, thoroughly RESEARCH the given Topic and Source Material. Do not skip this. A shallow script produces a failed video.

Research silently and establish:

Verified core facts — what actually happened, who was involved, where and when. Separate confirmed fact from legend, regional retelling, and popular myth.

The single strongest HOOK ANGLE — the most surprising, emotional, or high-stakes entry point a cold viewer would stop scrolling for.

The core EMOTION of this episode (one word) and the single PAYOFF the viewer gets at the end.

Visual opportunities — which 3–5 moments are inherently cinematic and what each looks like (era, location, costume, light, scale).

Uncertainties — anything sources disagree on or you cannot verify. NEVER invent quotations, Sanskrit verses, dates, statistics, dialogue from scripture, or miracles presented as scientific proof. Omit unsupported specifics or qualify them briefly.

Only after this research is solid, proceed to the workflow below. Source fidelity over invention — but emotion and clarity over dry recitation.

🕉️ RAMAYANA — ADI KAVYA
MASTER PROMPT FILE (Merged) — Version 8.0 HYBRID CINEMATIC (Scene 1 Video Hook)
Bible + Script Prompt + Hybrid Cinematic Production Prompt + Workflow Guide, in one document — Cinematic Video Hook Edition
This single file merges the original documents into one complete visual production system with a mandatory Scene 1 Video Hook to maximize viewer retention.

🏷️ THE THREE-TAG MASTER PROTOCOL (Narration + Visuals + Motion Graphics / Metadata)
This pipeline enforces a strict THREE-TAG SYSTEM:

1. Audio Narration Tag: Exactly one <script>...</script> block housing the clean TTS-ready narration in Section 2B. Spoken Devanagari Hindi only.

2. Sequential Visual Tags (Numbered Timeline):
- Scene 1 Hook: <video_prompt1>...</video_prompt1> — Mandatory 9:16 continuous cinematic video prompt (80–120 words) with camera movement to hook cold viewers immediately so they stay.
- Subsequent Story Stills: <image_prompt2>, <image_prompt3>, up to <image_prompt[N]> with real-time dynamic motion graphics.
- Thumbnail Tag: <image_prompt0> strictly reserved for the external promotional cover/thumbnail.
- Crucial Rule on <image_prompt0>: Index 0 is strictly reserved for the external promotional cover/thumbnail (16:9). It is never placed inside the video editing timeline.
- Story Stills: The actual narrative starts at <image_prompt1> and increments continuously through scene stills, the Follow Frame, and the End Card.

3. Real-Time Dynamic Motion Graphics Tags:
Sequential <motion_graphic1>, <motion_graphic2>, ... <motion_graphic[N]> (or <metadata[N]>) tags specifying real-time dynamic motion graphics.
The script AI decides in real time WHEN, WHERE, and WHICH TYPE of motion graphics is required based on the sacred story beats.
Crucial Rule: You are NOT limited to any template catalog or canned IDs! You can invent and specify ANY type of motion graphic that elevates the story (e.g. sacred_shloka_revelation, divine_astra_focus, celestial_timeline_dial, dharma_wisdom_punch, cosmic_metric_counter, sacred_vow_seal, etc.).

For each motion graphic, specify:
- #scene: The scene number where the graphic triggers
- Type: Any creative descriptive type chosen by the AI
- When: Exact contiguous cue phrase from the spoken narration that triggers the graphic
- Where: Screen placement (center, top, bottom, left, right, custom coordinates) respecting negative space
- Title: The primary headline or Sanskrit/Devanagari phrase
- Detail: Translation, spiritual meaning, or context
- Visual: Aesthetic styling and kinetic concept (e.g. 24k gold leaf calligraphy, luminous aura bloom, sacred vector linework, particle dissipation)

Example Format:
<motion_graphic1>
#scene 2
Type: sacred_vow_seal
When: [Exact contiguous spoken cue phrase from scene narration]
Where: top
Title: [Sacred Title / Mantra, e.g. उत्तिष्ठ राम]
Detail: [Spiritual context / meaning, e.g. तात जनक का संताप मिटाओ]
Visual: Sacred royal golden seal with radiant halo rays and glowing Devanagari lettering
</motion_graphic1>

All AI video, motion prompts, and animation directions are completely removed. Every visual asset is a detailed, static prompt.

PART 2 — 🕉️ THE BIBLE (Static Reference)
👥 CHARACTER BIBLE — NEVER CHANGE THESE DESCRIPTIONS
Copy relevant character details into EVERY image prompt.

🔵 RAMA
Age: 25–30 years old

Skin: Deep blue-dark complexion ("shyama varna") — non-negotiable, never fair

Face: Strong jaw, high forehead, calm and powerful eyes, slightly arched eyebrows

Body: Tall, broad shoulders, long arms reaching knees ("ajanubahu")

Hair: Long black hair tied in an ascetic knot (jata) or warrior bun

Palace attire: Yellow/gold silk dhoti, ornate crown (mukut), gold jewelry, bow Sharanga

Forest/Exile attire: Ochre/saffron bark-cloth dhoti, matted hair, no crown, bow and quiver

Expression: Dignified, compassionate, serene, divine majesty — never angry or anxious

🌟 SITA
Age: 20–25 years old

Skin: Golden-fair radiant complexion ("suvarna varna")

🗺️ LOCATION BIBLE
Ayodhya Palace: Treta Yuga Vedic stone architecture, colossal carved pillars, oil lamps, marigold drapes, sacred havan smoke, warm amber-gold light.

Dandaka / Panchavati Forest: Dense primordial Indian jungle, towering sal/banyan trees, hanging roots, morning mist, sacred thatched ashram hut with a quiet dhuni fire.

⚠️ RELIGIOUS ACCURACY LAW
Rama must always have blue-dark skin.

Treta Yuga setting only: absolute zero modern elements, modern clothing, or foreign architecture.

Sacred Vedic attributes (tilak, janeu, agni, mudras) must be visually accurate.

[ANCIENT DHARMA EDITORIAL RULES]
Apply these writing rules to Ancient Dharma episodes. For an explicitly unrelated topic, follow that topic's own tradition and audience instead of adding Hindu devotional language. These rules update the research, narration and closing instructions below; preserve every existing output section, extraction tag, asset number, media mode, character bible and narration-to-scene mapping. Perform the editorial work silently; do not add a new output section.

RESEARCH BEFORE COMMITTING TO A HOOK: Identify the actual source/version, what it supports, what belongs to a regional retelling, and what is interpretation. Establish one central dilemma, the strongest supported detail, the decisive choice and the real outcome. Treat any preselected retention hook as provisional: revise its wording and promise when the research does not support it. Never invent dialogue, motives, quotations, miracles as scientific proof, or scriptural attribution to make a hook work. Keep source notes in the existing production notes, with a brief natural attribution in speech where necessary.

OPEN INSIDE THE STORY: Compare three distinct, truthful openings internally: an action, a contradiction, and a consequential choice. Choose the clearest one, rather than always opening with a long 'why' question. Name the person or sacred object and make the situation understandable without the title. Match the first visible image/action to the first spoken words; no introductory temple montage or scenery before the predicament. The next sentence must advance that same event or give a useful clue, not restart with biography or a history lecture.

FORWARD MOMENTUM: Write simple, natural spoken Devanagari Hindi with devotional dignity. Every sentence must add necessary context, an action, discovery, obstacle, decision or consequence. Connect beats through cause and effect. Give intermediate answers; do not save every useful detail for the ending. Remove repeated praise, repeated explanations, abstract moral lectures, excessive adjectives and empty suspense. Preserve emotional breaths; never rush speech or add filler to satisfy a duration. Build emotion from supported events, not invented private thoughts.

SHORTS: Tell one complete dilemma and resolution, not an entire biography. Establish the concrete situation in the first short sentence and give a clue or consequence in the next one or two. Use a genuine discovery or consequential choice near the midpoint when the story needs it; do not force a twist or repeated question. Resolve the opening promise with the decisive action, reason and outcome, then move directly to the closing invitation.

ONE VARIED ENGAGEMENT CLOSE: After the complete story payoff, include ONE compact Hindi closing invitation asking viewers to like the video, subscribe to Ancient Dharma, and leave ONE specific comment. Allow approximately 5–8 seconds within the selected Shorts runtime; reserve this speech time before drafting the story. Do not try to squeeze all three requests into a three-second blessing. Keep it warm and direct, without interrupting the story or adding separate spoken like, subscribe, blessing and end-card sequences.

VARY THE COMMENT REQUEST: Choose either a short devotional response appropriate to the episode or one easy, concrete question about its central choice. Vary the response AND the sentence structure across topics; examples are alternatives, not a fixed closing to copy into every video. Ram-focused episodes may invite 'जय श्री राम' or 'सीताराम'; Hanuman-focused episodes may invite 'जय बजरंगबली' or 'जय हनुमान'; Shiva-focused episodes may invite 'हर हर महादेव' or 'ॐ नमः शिवाय'; Krishna-focused episodes may invite 'राधे कृष्ण' or 'जय श्री कृष्ण'. Never force a Ram greeting into an unrelated tradition. For a dilemma, ask a brief question such as 'भरत के किस निर्णय ने आपको सबसे अधिक छुआ?' instead of a generic 'आपकी क्या राय है?'. Invite one response, not a list of questions.

Possible closing patterns, adapted to the episode rather than repeated verbatim: 'कमेंट में जय श्री राम लिखिए। कथा अच्छी लगी तो लाइक करें और Ancient Dharma को सब्सक्राइब करें।' / 'हनुमान जी की भक्ति को नमन—कमेंट में जय बजरंगबली! ऐसी कथाओं के लिए लाइक करें और चैनल सब्सक्राइब करें।' / 'भरत के किस निर्णय ने आपका मन छुआ? कमेंट में बताइए, वीडियो लाइक करें और चैनल से जुड़ने के लिए सब्सक्राइब करें।' Use natural Hindi pronunciation of the channel name in speech if needed. Make the invitation compelling through relevance, never guilt, threats, guaranteed blessings, promised miracles, or claims that a 'true devotee' must engage. Do not demand repeated comments, personal information, or a subscription in exchange for the answer.

SYNC AND SILENT CHECK: Put the closing words exactly once in the clean voice script and their matching final CTA narration segment(s), using the existing tags and timeline format. Reuse existing follow/end-card slots where present; they form one close, not additional speeches or silent padding. Overlays must match the selected comment request and must not add conflicting engagement demands. Check that the opening is specific, the next sentence advances it, the source supports the claim, the middle develops, the payoff is complete before the CTA, and the close includes like + subscribe + one episode-relevant comment invitation. Do not output these checks or predict retention scores.
[/ANCIENT DHARMA EDITORIAL RULES]

PART 3 — 🕉️ SCRIPT PROMPT (Creative Pass — Run FIRST)
Take raw content and output a locked Hindi script. Never generate images or visual prompts in this pass.

Content Setup & Rules
Hook Rule: The first 3–6 spoken words must begin a concrete, source-supported action, dilemma or contrast with immediate emotional stakes. Complete a clear opening thought within the first 1–3 seconds; name the relevant person or sacred object instead of a vague "this" or "he". Let the unanswered question arise from why the action matters, not from hiding who is involved. No channel greetings, series titles, background lecture or invented sacred dialogue. Keep the central question clear while giving an early concrete answer, clue or consequence in the next one or two sentences. Every following sentence must change what the viewer knows, what the protagonist can do, or what the choice will cost. Connect beats through cause and effect; cut repeated setup, biography before the predicament, redundant adjectives and generic suspense. Aim for a meaningful development about every 5–8 seconds where the story supports it, inside the existing scene structure; this is a writing guide, not a cut, scene-count or speech-speed requirement. Use short, natural spoken sentences, clear subjects and concrete verbs. Never hide basic context just to manufacture curiosity. Silently compare three different opening lines and use the clearest, most specific one that the story actually pays off; output only the chosen line in the existing format. Read the opening without the title: the viewer must understand the situation and have a specific reason to hear the next sentence. Remove any line that adds neither necessary context nor a new development. These are editorial choices, not guaranteed audience metrics.

Midpoint Re-Hook: At 50–60% mark, use a concise source-supported discovery, decision or consequence that changes the meaning of an earlier detail or raises the cost of the next action. Follow the 5–8 word turn with its concrete explanation; do not merely announce that a twist is coming. Preserve devotional dignity and source fidelity. A smaller resolved question should lead naturally into the remaining central question.

Language: Simple, poignant, spoken Devanagari Hindi with temple-katha resonance.

Ending: Complete the story and its promised payoff first. Then give ONE varied Hindi closing invitation to like, subscribe and leave one episode-relevant comment, following the editorial rules above. Reserve approximately 5–8 seconds within the selected runtime. Use the existing follow/end-card slots as one close; no separate repeated blessing, recap or extra engagement requests. Finish the story on its concrete consequence before the invitation.

graphics.style: Let AI choose only moments where a graphic materially explains the narration. Metadata is a suggestion, never a command to decorate every scene. Leave ordinary footage clean, keep breathing room between beats, and allow zero graphics. No cards, panels, boxed labels, enclosing frames, blur backings or photo badges. Use free-floating type, fine lines and purposeful diagrams in open space around subjects. Never invent facts, coordinates, source labels or telemetry. Preview the actual result before export.

### ⚖️ MANDATORY 50/50 MEDIA SPLIT (50% VIDEO / 50% IMAGE)
Every episode must maintain an exact 50/50 split between static image scenes and moving video scenes across the entire duration.

[ANCIENT DHARMA EDITORIAL RULES]
Apply these writing rules to Ancient Dharma episodes. For an explicitly unrelated topic, follow that topic's own tradition and audience instead of adding Hindu devotional language. These rules update the research, narration and closing instructions below; preserve every existing output section, extraction tag, asset number, media mode, character bible and narration-to-scene mapping. Perform the editorial work silently; do not add a new output section.

RESEARCH BEFORE COMMITTING TO A HOOK: Identify the actual source/version, what it supports, what belongs to a regional retelling, and what is interpretation. Establish one central dilemma, the strongest supported detail, the decisive choice and the real outcome. Treat any preselected retention hook as provisional: revise its wording and promise when the research does not support it. Never invent dialogue, motives, quotations, miracles as scientific proof, or scriptural attribution to make a hook work. Keep source notes in the existing production notes, with a brief natural attribution in speech where necessary.

OPEN INSIDE THE STORY: Compare three distinct, truthful openings internally: an action, a contradiction, and a consequential choice. Choose the clearest one, rather than always opening with a long 'why' question. Name the person or sacred object and make the situation understandable without the title. Match the first visible image/action to the first spoken words; no introductory temple montage or scenery before the predicament. The next sentence must advance that same event or give a useful clue, not restart with biography or a history lecture.

FORWARD MOMENTUM: Write simple, natural spoken Devanagari Hindi with devotional dignity. Every sentence must add necessary context, an action, discovery, obstacle, decision or consequence. Connect beats through cause and effect. Give intermediate answers; do not save every useful detail for the ending. Remove repeated praise, repeated explanations, abstract moral lectures, excessive adjectives and empty suspense. Preserve emotional breaths; never rush speech or add filler to satisfy a duration. Build emotion from supported events, not invented private thoughts.

SHORTS: Tell one complete dilemma and resolution, not an entire biography. Establish the concrete situation in the first short sentence and give a clue or consequence in the next one or two. Use a genuine discovery or consequential choice near the midpoint when the story needs it; do not force a twist or repeated question. Resolve the opening promise with the decisive action, reason and outcome, then move directly to the closing invitation.

ONE VARIED ENGAGEMENT CLOSE: After the complete story payoff, include ONE compact Hindi closing invitation asking viewers to like the video, subscribe to Ancient Dharma, and leave ONE specific comment. Allow approximately 5–8 seconds within the selected Shorts runtime; reserve this speech time before drafting the story. Do not try to squeeze all three requests into a three-second blessing. Keep it warm and direct, without interrupting the story or adding separate spoken like, subscribe, blessing and end-card sequences.

VARY THE COMMENT REQUEST: Choose either a short devotional response appropriate to the episode or one easy, concrete question about its central choice. Vary the response AND the sentence structure across topics; examples are alternatives, not a fixed closing to copy into every video. Ram-focused episodes may invite 'जय श्री राम' or 'सीताराम'; Hanuman-focused episodes may invite 'जय बजरंगबली' or 'जय हनुमान'; Shiva-focused episodes may invite 'हर हर महादेव' or 'ॐ नमः शिवाय'; Krishna-focused episodes may invite 'राधे कृष्ण' or 'जय श्री कृष्ण'. Never force a Ram greeting into an unrelated tradition. For a dilemma, ask a brief question such as 'भरत के किस निर्णय ने आपको सबसे अधिक छुआ?' instead of a generic 'आपकी क्या राय है?'. Invite one response, not a list of questions.

Possible closing patterns, adapted to the episode rather than repeated verbatim: 'कमेंट में जय श्री राम लिखिए। कथा अच्छी लगी तो लाइक करें और Ancient Dharma को सब्सक्राइब करें।' / 'हनुमान जी की भक्ति को नमन—कमेंट में जय बजरंगबली! ऐसी कथाओं के लिए लाइक करें और चैनल सब्सक्राइब करें।' / 'भरत के किस निर्णय ने आपका मन छुआ? कमेंट में बताइए, वीडियो लाइक करें और चैनल से जुड़ने के लिए सब्सक्राइब करें।' Use natural Hindi pronunciation of the channel name in speech if needed. Make the invitation compelling through relevance, never guilt, threats, guaranteed blessings, promised miracles, or claims that a 'true devotee' must engage. Do not demand repeated comments, personal information, or a subscription in exchange for the answer.

SYNC AND SILENT CHECK: Put the closing words exactly once in the clean voice script and their matching final CTA narration segment(s), using the existing tags and timeline format. Reuse existing follow/end-card slots where present; they form one close, not additional speeches or silent padding. Overlays must match the selected comment request and must not add conflicting engagement demands. Check that the opening is specific, the next sentence advances it, the source supports the claim, the middle develops, the payoff is complete before the CTA, and the close includes like + subscribe + one episode-relevant comment invitation. Do not output these checks or predict retention scores.
[/ANCIENT DHARMA EDITORIAL RULES]

PART 3 — 🕉️ SCRIPT PROMPT (Creative Pass — Run FIRST)Take raw content and output a locked Hindi script. Define asset types for every single beat.Script Architecture Rules:Hook Rule: The first 3–6 spoken words must begin a concrete, source-supported action, dilemma or contrast with immediate emotional stakes. Complete a clear opening thought within the first 1–3 seconds; name the relevant person or sacred object instead of a vague "this" or "he". Let the unanswered question arise from why the action matters, not from hiding who is involved. No channel greetings, series titles, background lecture or invented sacred dialogue. Keep the central question clear while giving an early concrete answer, clue or consequence in the next one or two sentences. Every following sentence must change what the viewer knows, what the protagonist can do, or what the choice will cost. Connect beats through cause and effect; cut repeated setup, biography before the predicament, redundant adjectives and generic suspense. Aim for a meaningful development about every 5–8 seconds where the story supports it, inside the existing scene structure; this is a writing guide, not a cut, scene-count or speech-speed requirement. Use short, natural spoken sentences, clear subjects and concrete verbs. Never hide basic context just to manufacture curiosity. Silently compare three different opening lines and use the clearest, most specific one that the story actually pays off; output only the chosen line in the existing format. Read the opening without the title: the viewer must understand the situation and have a specific reason to hear the next sentence. Remove any line that adds neither necessary context nor a new development. These are editorial choices, not guaranteed audience metrics.Midpoint Re-Hook: At 50–60% mark, use a concise source-supported discovery, decision or consequence that changes the meaning of an earlier detail or raises the cost of the next action. Follow the 5–8 word turn with its concrete explanation; do not merely announce that a twist is coming. Preserve devotional dignity and source fidelity. A smaller resolved question should lead naturally into the remaining central question.Language: Simple, poignant, spoken Devanagari Hindi with temple-katha resonance.Ending: Complete the story and its promised payoff first. Then give ONE varied Hindi closing invitation to like, subscribe and leave one episode-relevant comment, following the editorial rules above. Reserve approximately 5–8 seconds within the selected runtime. Use the existing follow/end-card slots as one close; no separate repeated blessing, recap or extra engagement requests. Finish the story on its concrete consequence before the invitation.
